sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Structural questions ask two things: what forces and deflections does a structure experience, and is a given steel or concrete member strong enough?

The analysis half is statics and mechanics of materials applied to whole beams, trusses and frames. The design half adds load factors and the capacity formulas for steel and reinforced concrete.
pitfalls: Comparing a factored load with a nominal strength without applying the strength reduction factor.
Using actual length instead of effective length for a column whose ends are not pinned.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Structural Analysis Review Session 2022
items: At a pin joining two members, the forces on the two members are equal and opposite.
Do not forget the moment. A fixed support and a cut through a beam both carry a moment as well as forces.
Fixed-end moments for standard loads are in the handbook; for a point load they are P a b^{2} / L^{2} and P a^{2} b / L^{2}.
If an answer is off by a factor of 1,000 or 12, the units are the first thing to check.
Concrete beams are designed to be tension-controlled: the steel strain reaches at least 0.005 so that failure is ductile, which is what allows the 0.90 strength reduction factor.
In U.S. units the concrete formulas that take a square root of the strength expect it in psi, not ksi.
For shear, add the concrete and stirrup contributions, apply the reduction factor and compare with the factored shear.

bridge.plain: Structural engineering works out the forces that loads cause in beams, columns, trusses and frames, and then checks that steel or concrete members are strong and stiff enough.
core: Loads follow a path: floor to beam to column to foundation.
Analysis finds internal forces: axial force, shear and bending moment.
Design compares a factored load effect with a reduced strength.
Slender columns fail by buckling before the material is crushed.
bridge.links: It applies statics (reactions, trusses) and mechanics of materials (stress, deflection, buckling), and uses material strengths. Foundations hand the loads to geotechnics.

sections.title: Analysis of statically determinate beams, columns, trusses and frames
sections.body:
A structure is statically determinate when the equations of equilibrium alone give every reaction and internal force. Analysis is statics applied in order: find the reactions, then cut the structure where you want the internal force and balance one of the pieces.

For beams the results are shear and moment at each section. For trusses they are axial forces in members, by joints or by sections. For frames, separate the members at their connections and remember that the force one member puts on another is equal and opposite.

formulas.name: Simple span, point load at a from left

pitfalls: Taking the maximum moment at midspan for an off-centre load.
Stopping at a force component when the member force is asked for.

ideas.title: Slide a force along its line of action
ideas.text: A force gives the same moment wherever it is placed along its own line. Move it to the point where one of its components passes through the moment centre, and that component drops out.

ideas.title: Sections through a truss
ideas.text: With parallel chords, summing vertical forces on the cut piece gives the diagonal directly. With sloping chords, take moments about the point where the other two cut members meet.

ideas.title: Split a frame at its internal pins
ideas.text: Pin forces show up only when the members are separated. They are equal and opposite on the two pieces, so solve the simpler piece first and carry its pin force, reversed, to the other.

ideas.title: Shearing force and bending moment
ideas.text: A cantilever resists load through shear and moment at its fixed end. For a tip load the moment grows linearly from zero at the free end to P L at the support.

ideas.title: Shearing force and bending moment
ideas.text: Reactions from several loads can be found one load at a time and added (superposition). The uniform load splits equally; the point load splits in inverse proportion to its distance from each support.

ideas.title: Shearing force and bending moment
ideas.text: With a central point load each reaction is P/2, and the moment under the load is the reaction times half the span: M_{max} = P L / 4.

examples.problem: A cantilever beam is 3.5 m long and carries a 24 kN point load at its free end. What is the magnitude of the bending moment at the fixed support?
examples.idea: A cantilever resists load through shear and moment at its fixed end. For a tip load the moment grows linearly from zero at the free end to P L at the support.
examples.steps: M = P L = 24 × 3.5 = 84 kN·m at the fixed support (tension on the top face).

examples.problem: A simply supported beam spans 12 m. It carries a uniform load of 3 kN/m over the full span and a 30 kN point load 4 m from the left support. What is the left reaction?
examples.idea: Reactions from several loads can be found one load at a time and added (superposition). The uniform load splits equally; the point load splits in inverse proportion to its distance from each support.
examples.steps:
From the uniform load: 3(12) / 2 = 18 kN.

From the point load: 30 × \frac{12 - 4}{12} = 20.00 kN.

Left reaction = 18 + 20.00 = 38.0 kN.

examples.idea: With a central point load each reaction is P/2, and the moment under the load is the reaction times half the span: M_{max} = P L / 4.

M_{max} = 25 × 6 = \frac{P L}{4} = 150 kN·m, under the load.

examples.problem: A simply supported beam spans 8 m. A clockwise couple of 162 kN·m is applied to it at midspan and there are no other loads. What is the magnitude of each support reaction?
examples.idea: A couple has no net force, so the two reactions must form an equal and opposite couple: one up, one down, each equal to the applied moment divided by the span. Where the couple is applied does not change the reactions.
examples.steps: R = \frac{M_{0}}{L} = \frac{162}{8} = 20.25 kN, upward at one support and downward at the other.

examples.problem: A simply supported beam spans 6.8 m and carries a triangular load that is zero at one end and 14 kN/m at the other. What is the maximum bending moment?

sections.deep:
Analysing a determinate structure means finding reactions and then internal forces, with equilibrium alone. Beams carry load by shear and bending, trusses by axial force in their members and frames by a combination. The standard cases are worth knowing by heart: a simple span with a central load has a maximum moment of P L / 4, with a uniform load w L^{2} / 8, and a cantilever P L or w L^{2} / 2 at the support.

Moving loads are handled with influence lines, which show how a reaction, shear or moment at one location varies as a unit load crosses the structure.
method: Draw the free-body diagram and find reactions.
Cut the structure where the internal force is wanted and apply equilibrium to one side.
For a truss, use joints or sections.
For maximum effects, place loads where the influence line ordinates are largest.
Check with a known standard case when one applies.

sections.title: Deflection of statically determinate beams, trusses and frames
sections.body:
Deflection is how far a structure moves under load. Codes limit it so that floors do not bounce and finishes do not crack. Deflection grows with load and very quickly with span, and shrinks with stiffness EI.

Use the tabulated beam cases in the handbook for standard loadings and add the results when several loads act together (superposition). For trusses and unusual cases, the unit load (virtual work) method applies a dummy unit load where the deflection is wanted.
pitfalls: Unit mix-ups: keep everything in kN and m, or N and mm.
Forgetting that span is raised to the third or fourth power.
Using a beam table case that matches the loading but not the supports, or misreading how the table defines L.
Mixing feet and inches in w L^{4} / (E I). With w in kips per foot and L in feet, the result needs a factor of 12^{3} to come out in inches.

sections.deep:
Deflection depends on load, span, stiffness EI and support conditions. Span has by far the largest effect: deflection varies with the cube of span for a point load and the fourth power for a uniform load. The handbook tabulates slopes and deflections for standard cases, and superposition lets you add cases for combined loads.

Other methods derive the same results: double integration of M / EI, the moment-area theorems, and the unit load (virtual work) method, which also handles trusses by summing F f L / (A E) over the members.
method: Match the beam and load to a table case.
Convert units so that EI and the loads are consistent.
Substitute and compute the deflection.
For several loads, compute each separately and add.
For a truss joint, apply the unit load method.

sections.title: Column analysis
sections.body:
A short, stocky column fails when its material crushes. A long, slender column fails earlier by buckling: it suddenly bows sideways. Euler's formula gives the buckling load. It depends on stiffness EI and falls with the square of the effective length.

How the ends are held changes the effective length. Pinned at both ends, K is 1.0. Fixed at both ends, 0.5. Fixed at one end and pinned at the other, 0.7. Fixed at the base and free at the top, 2.0. A column buckles about its weaker axis unless bracing prevents it.
pitfalls: Using the stronger-axis moment of inertia when the weak axis governs.
Forgetting the effective length factor.
Checking only the weak axis when the two axes have different unbraced lengths.

ideas.title: One load, two ways to buckle
ideas.text: The same axial load could buckle the column about either axis, each with its own effective length and moment of inertia. Compute both critical loads; the smaller governs. Bracing the weak axis at mid-height quarters its slenderness effect, so the strong axis can end up governing.

ideas.title: Euler's formula
ideas.text: A slender column fails by elastic buckling at the Euler load, P_{cr} = π^{2} E I / (K L)^{2}. Pinned ends give K = 1. Buckling happens about the axis with the smaller moment of inertia.

ideas.title: Effective length
ideas.text: The effective length K L is the length of the equivalent pinned-pinned column, the distance between inflection points of the buckled shape. End restraint shortens it: K = 0.5 fixed-fixed, 0.7 fixed-pinned, 1.0 pinned-pinned, 2.0 fixed-free.

ideas.text: One axial load can buckle the column about either axis. Each axis has its own unbraced length and moment of inertia, and the smaller critical load governs. Bracing the weak axis at mid-height halves its length and quadruples its critical load.

examples.idea: One axial load can buckle the column about either axis. Each axis has its own unbraced length and moment of inertia, and the smaller critical load governs. Bracing the weak axis at mid-height halves its length and quadruples its critical load.
examples.steps:
Strong axis, full length: P = \frac{π^{2}(200,000)(60 × 10^{6})}{(7,000)^{2}} = 2,417 kN.

Weak axis, half length: P = \frac{π^{2}(200,000)(12 × 10^{6})}{(3,500)^{2}} = 1,934 kN.

The smaller governs: 1,934 kN.

examples.problem: A column has a slenderness ratio (effective length over radius of gyration) of 105 and a modulus of elasticity of 200 GPa. What is its Euler critical stress?
examples.idea: Dividing the Euler load by the area gives a critical stress of π^{2} E / (KL/r)^{2}. It depends only on stiffness and slenderness, not on the material's strength, and it applies only while it is below the proportional limit.

sections.deep:
Columns fail either by crushing or by buckling, depending on slenderness. Euler's formula gives the elastic buckling load of a slender column as pi^{2} E I / (K L)^{2}. The effective length K L accounts for end conditions: restraint against rotation shortens it and freedom to sway lengthens it.

Buckling happens about the axis with the larger slenderness ratio K L / r, usually the weak axis unless bracing changes the unbraced lengths. Short columns are governed by material strength, and design specifications blend the two regimes.
method: Identify the end conditions and the effective length factor K.
Compute K L / r for each axis with its own unbraced length.
Use the larger slenderness ratio.
Apply Euler's formula for the critical load, or divide by area for critical stress.
Check that the critical stress is below yield; otherwise Euler does not apply.

sections.title: Structural determinacy and stability
sections.body:
Counting tells you whether statics alone can solve a structure. Compare the number of unknown forces with the number of equilibrium equations. Equal means determinate. More unknowns means indeterminate, by the difference. Fewer means unstable.

For a planar truss there are two equations per joint and the unknowns are the member forces plus the reactions. For a beam or frame there are three equations per free body, plus one for each internal hinge. Passing the count does not guarantee stability: reactions that are all parallel or all meet at one point leave the structure free to move.

formulas.name: Beam
formulas.expr: r compared with 3 + number of internal hinges

pitfalls: Assuming a structure is stable just because the count balances.

example.problem: A truss has 10 joints, 17 members and 3 reactions. Classify it.
example.steps: m + r = 20 and 2j = 20, so it is statically determinate, if stable.

ideas.title: Stability of a gravity dam
ideas.text: A gravity dam is checked as a rigid block on a unit length. Against sliding, compare the friction available, coefficient times weight, with the water thrust, half the unit weight of water times depth squared. Against overturning, compare the moment of the weight about the toe with the moment of the water thrust, which acts at one third of the depth.

ideas.title: Beams and frames
ideas.text: A rigid body in a plane has three equilibrium equations. With r reaction components and n bodies: r = 3n is statically determinate, r greater than 3n is indeterminate to the degree r - 3n, and r less than 3n is unstable. Each internal hinge adds one condition equation.

ideas.title: Trusses
ideas.text: For a plane truss with m members, r reactions and j joints, each joint gives two equations. m + r = 2j is determinate, m + r greater than 2j is indeterminate to the degree m + r - 2j, and m + r less than 2j is unstable.

ideas.title: Counting is necessary, not sufficient
ideas.text: A structure that passes the count can still be unstable if its reactions are all parallel or all pass through one point, or if a panel can deform without stressing any member. Check the geometry as well as the count.

ideas.title: Why the class matters
ideas.text: A determinate structure is solved with equilibrium alone and is unaffected by support settlement or temperature. An indeterminate one also needs compatibility of deformations, but its redundancy gives alternative load paths.

examples.problem: A rigid plane frame has 3 members, 4 joints and 8 support reaction components, with no internal hinges. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
examples.idea: For a rigid plane frame each member carries three unknown internal forces and each joint supplies three equilibrium equations: degree = 3m + r - 3j. Zero means determinate; a positive value is the number of extra unknowns.

sections.deep:
Before analysing a structure, establish whether equilibrium alone can solve it. Count the unknowns and the equations. If they match and the supports are properly arranged, it is statically determinate. Extra unknowns make it indeterminate, and too few supports make it unstable.

Stability is also a matter of geometry. Three reactions that are parallel or that meet at one point cannot hold a body, whatever the count says.
method: Count reaction components: roller 1, pin 2, fixed 3.
For a beam or frame compare with 3 equations per rigid part, adding one per internal hinge.
For a truss compare m + r with 2j.
State the degree of indeterminacy as the excess of unknowns.
Look for parallel or concurrent reactions that make the structure unstable.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A structure must have enough supports and members to stay put, and it is determinate when the unknown forces are exactly as many as the balance equations. Counting unknowns against equations gives the answer.

the state of an object that is not accelerating: all forces on it cancel, and so do all their turning effects
reaction

unit weight

moment

sections.title: Elementary statically indeterminate structures
sections.body:
An indeterminate structure has more supports or members than statics can solve for. The extra equations come from how the structure deforms. The force method removes a redundant support, finds the deflection there, and then finds the force needed to push it back to zero.

A few standard results are worth knowing. A propped cantilever under uniform load puts three eighths of the load on the prop. A beam fixed at both ends under uniform load has end moments of wL^{2}/12 and a midspan moment of wL^{2}/24. Stiffer parts attract more load.
pitfalls: Using simple-span formulas for a beam with fixed ends.
Sharing load to supports by tributary length on a continuous beam. On two equal spans under uniform load the middle support carries 1.25 w L, not w L.

example.problem: A fixed-fixed beam spans 4 m with 9 kN/m. Find the end moment.

ideas.title: The redundant as a correcting force
ideas.text: Remove the extra support and let the beam deflect there under the load. The redundant reaction is the force that pushes that point back to zero deflection. With constant E I the stiffness cancels out of the result.

ideas.title: Cantilevered beam slopes and deflections
ideas.text: A propped cantilever has one more reaction than statics can solve, so a compatibility condition is needed: the deflection at the roller is zero. Setting the downward deflection from the load, w L^{4} / (8 EI), equal to the upward deflection from the reaction, R L^{3} / (3 EI), gives R = 3 w L / 8.

ideas.title: Fixed-end moment
ideas.text: Fixed ends prevent rotation, which attracts negative moment to the supports. For a full uniform load the fixed-end moment is w L^{2} / 12 and the midspan moment drops to w L^{2} / 24; together they still add to the simple-span value w L^{2} / 8.

ideas.title: Fixed-end moment
ideas.text: Fixed-end moments are the support moments of a beam held against rotation at both ends. For a point load they are P a b^{2} / L^{2} at the end a distance a from the load and P a^{2} b / L^{2} at the other end. The end nearer the load takes the larger moment, and for a central load both equal P L / 8.

ideas.title: Indeterminate
ideas.text: A two-span continuous beam is indeterminate to the first degree. Removing the middle support and restoring zero deflection there gives a middle reaction of 1.25 w L, more than the w L that tributary length would suggest; each end support carries 0.375 w L.

examples.problem: A beam 10 m long is fixed at one end and supported by a roller at the other. It carries a uniform load of 12 kN/m. What is the reaction at the roller?
examples.idea: A propped cantilever has one more reaction than statics can solve, so a compatibility condition is needed: the deflection at the roller is zero. Setting the downward deflection from the load, w L^{4} / (8 EI), equal to the upward deflection from the reaction, R L^{3} / (3 EI), gives R = 3 w L / 8.
examples.steps: \frac{R L^{3}}{3 EI} = \frac{w L^{4}}{8 EI}, so R = \frac{3 w L}{8} = \frac{3(12)(10)}{8} = 45 kN. The fixed end carries the other 75 kN.

sections.deep:
An indeterminate structure has more supports or members than equilibrium needs, so deformations must be brought in. The force method removes a redundant support, computes the deflection there, then finds the redundant force that restores zero deflection. Fixed-end moments and standard cases in the handbook give the results for common beams directly.

Stiffness attracts load: when members share a load, the stiffer one takes more. That principle explains moment distribution and why fixed ends reduce midspan moment while adding support moment.
method: Identify the redundant reaction.
Remove it and compute the deflection at that point from the applied loads.
Compute the deflection there caused by a unit value of the redundant.
Solve for the redundant that makes the total deflection zero.
Finish with equilibrium for the remaining reactions.

sections.title: Loads, load combinations and load paths
sections.body:
Structures carry dead load (their own weight and fixed items), live load (people, furniture, vehicles), and environmental loads such as wind, snow and earthquake. A load path is the route a load takes to the ground: slab to beam to girder to column to footing. Each member carries the load from its tributary area.

Design codes combine loads with factors that reflect how uncertain each one is. In LRFD the common gravity combinations are 1.4D and 1.2D + 1.6L, and the largest result governs. An influence line shows how a force at one point changes as a unit load moves across the structure, and is used to place moving loads for the worst effect.
pitfalls: Forgetting to check every combination and take the largest.
Skipping the live load reduction when the tributary area is large enough for it to apply.

example.problem: A column supports a tributary area of 36 m^{2} with D = 5 kPa and L = 3 kPa. Find the governing factored load.

ideas.title: Tributary area is a watershed
ideas.text: A beam collects the floor load from halfway out to the neighbouring beam on each side, as a river collects rain from its watershed. Multiply the area load by that width to get the line load.

ideas.title: Live load reduction
ideas.text: A large floor area is unlikely to carry its full live load everywhere at once, so the code allows the live load on members with a large tributary area to be reduced before the load combinations are applied. The handbook gives the formula and its limits.

ideas.title: Load combinations
ideas.text: In strength design (LRFD) each load is multiplied by a load factor that reflects its uncertainty, and the largest combination governs. Live load has the larger factor because it is less predictable than dead load.

ideas.title: Tributary area
ideas.text: A beam collects floor load from its tributary width, half the spacing on each side. Line load = area load × tributary width.

ideas.title: Load combinations
ideas.text: Follow the load path. Factor the area loads, multiply by the tributary width (the beam spacing for an interior beam) to get a line load, then use the simple-span moment w L^{2} / 8.

examples.problem: A floor beam carries a dead load of 25 kN/m and a live load of 35 kN/m. Checking the load combinations 1.4D and 1.2D + 1.6L, what factored load governs?
examples.idea: In strength design (LRFD) each load is multiplied by a load factor that reflects its uncertainty, and the largest combination governs. Live load has the larger factor because it is less predictable than dead load.
examples.steps:

1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(25) + 1.6(35) = 86 kN/m.

The larger value governs: 86 kN/m.

Loads are classified by source: dead, live, roof live, snow, wind, earthquake and others. Design combines them with load factors that reflect how uncertain each is and how unlikely it is that several peak together. The load path is the route by which load travels to the ground: slab to beam to girder to column to footing. Each member collects load from its tributary area, and following the path is how line loads and column loads are found.
method: List the service loads acting on the member.
Find tributary width or area and convert area loads to line or point loads.
Evaluate each applicable load combination.
Take the largest factored effect for design.
Follow the reactions down to the next member in the load path.

sections.title: Design of steel components
sections.body:
Steel design compares a factored load with a design strength: the nominal strength times a resistance factor. Tension members are checked for yielding on the gross area and for fracture on the net area at the bolt holes.

Beams that are compact and braced against sideways buckling can reach their full plastic moment, the yield stress times the plastic section modulus. Columns are governed by buckling, so their strength depends on the slenderness ratio. Connections are checked for bolt shear, bearing and weld strength.
pitfalls: Using the elastic section modulus S where the plastic modulus Z is required.
Checking only yielding and skipping fracture on the net section.

example.problem: A plate with a gross area of 1,500 mm^{2} has F_{y} = 250 MPa. Find the design tensile strength for yielding.

ideas.title: Two ways a tension member fails
ideas.text: Yielding is checked on the gross area away from the holes, with a resistance factor of 0.90. Rupture is checked on the effective net area through the holes, with 0.75. Compare the two after applying the factors; the smaller governs. The hole deduction is the hole diameter plus 1/16 in for damage.

ideas.title: Columns with different lengths about each axis
ideas.text: Compare K L / r for each axis and use the larger. The design tables are built on the weak axis, so a strong-axis length is converted to its weak-axis equivalent by dividing by r_{x} / r_{y}.

ideas.title: Beam strength falls with unbraced length
ideas.text: A fully braced compact beam reaches its plastic moment. As the unbraced length grows past a first limit, the compression flange starts to buckle sideways and strength drops in a straight line; past a second limit the buckling is elastic and strength falls faster. A moment gradient factor raises the curve but never above the plastic moment.

ideas.title: Tension members
ideas.text: Tension yielding is checked on the gross area: nominal strength P_{n} = F_{y} A_{g}, and design strength is the resistance factor times P_{n}. Rupture on the net section is a separate check with a factor of 0.75.

ideas.title: AISC
ideas.text: A compact, laterally braced beam can reach its full plastic moment, M_{p} = F_{y} Z, where every fibre has yielded. The design strength is the resistance factor times M_{p}.

ideas.title: Slenderness
ideas.text: The slenderness ratio K L / r measures how prone a column is to buckling; the larger it is, the lower the critical stress. Use the radius of gyration for the axis about which buckling occurs, with both lengths in the same units.

ideas.title: Tension members
ideas.text: Rupture is checked on the net area through the holes. Each hole removes a width equal to the bolt diameter plus 1/8 in: 1/16 in for the standard hole and 1/16 in for damage. Design strength is 0.75 F_{u} A_{e}, with A_{e} = U A_{n}.

examples.problem: A steel tension member has a gross area of 2,800 mm^{2} and a yield strength of 345 MPa. Using LRFD with a resistance factor of 0.90, what is its design strength for yielding on the gross section?

sections.deep:
Steel design checks each limit state: a design strength, the resistance factor times nominal strength, must be at least the factored load effect. Tension members are checked for yielding on the gross area and rupture on the effective net area. Compression members are governed by buckling, through the slenderness ratio. Beams that are compact and braced reach the plastic moment F_{y} Z; without adequate bracing, lateral-torsional buckling reduces the strength.

Shear, deflection and connections are separate checks. Allowable strength design divides nominal strength by a safety factor instead and uses unfactored load combinations.
method: Identify the member type and the limit states that apply.
Compute the nominal strength for each limit state.
Multiply by the resistance factor: 0.90 for yielding, flexure and compression, 0.75 for rupture.
Compare the smallest design strength with the factored demand.
Check serviceability under unfactored loads.

terms: factored
multiplied by a load factor greater than 1, to give a design load with a safety margin
design strength
nominal strength multiplied by a resistance factor less than 1; it must be at least the factored load effect
nominal
calculated from the code formula before any safety factor is applied
buckling
sudden sideways bowing of a slender member in compression, at a load below what would crush the material
plastic moment
the moment at which a steel section has yielded through its full depth
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
section modulus
moment of inertia divided by the distance to the outer edge; bending stress is moment divided by it
slenderness ratio
effective length divided by radius of gyration; a high value means the column buckles easily
radius of gyration
the distance from an axis at which the whole area (or mass) could be concentrated and keep the same moment of inertia

sections.title: Design of reinforced concrete components
sections.body:
Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, so steel bars are placed where tension occurs. In a beam, the concrete near the top is squeezed and the steel near the bottom is stretched. The two forces are equal and form a couple that resists the moment.

The compressed concrete is modelled as a rectangular block at 0.85 of the concrete strength. Its depth comes from setting the concrete force equal to the steel force. The design strength is the nominal strength times a reduction factor: 0.90 for tension-controlled bending and 0.75 for shear. Shear is carried by the concrete and by stirrups.
pitfalls: Using the overall depth h instead of the effective depth d.
Forgetting the strength reduction factor when the question asks for design strength.
Leaving the moment in kip-inches, or forgetting the strength reduction factor, when the question asks for design strength in kip-feet.

ideas.title: Why beams are under-reinforced
ideas.text: With a modest amount of steel the bars yield before the concrete crushes, so the beam sags and cracks visibly before it fails. With too much steel the concrete crushes first, without warning, and the code penalises that with a lower strength reduction factor.

ideas.title: Stirrups
ideas.text: Shear strength is the concrete's contribution plus the stirrups' contribution, A_{v} f_{y} d / s, where A_{v} counts both legs of the stirrup. Stirrups are needed once the factored shear exceeds half the reduced concrete strength, and their spacing is capped at d / 2 so that a diagonal crack cannot pass between them.

ideas.title: Design strength of a tied column
ideas.text: For a short tied column, the design axial strength is 0.80 × 0.65 × (0.85 f'_{c} (A_{g} - A_{st}) + f_{y} A_{st}). The 0.65 is the reduction factor for compression and the 0.80 allows for accidental eccentricity.

ideas.title: ACI 318
ideas.text: At nominal strength the steel force T = A_{s} f_{y} is balanced by a rectangular concrete stress block of intensity 0.85 f'_{c} and depth a. The moment capacity is that force times the lever arm between them, d - a/2.

ideas.title: ACI 318
ideas.text: Horizontal equilibrium of the section sets the stress block depth: the concrete compression 0.85 f'_{c} a b equals the steel tension A_{s} f_{y}.

ideas.title: ACI 318
ideas.text: The concrete contribution to shear strength depends on the square root of the compressive strength, because shear failure is governed by diagonal tension, and on the web area b d.

ideas.title: ACI 318
ideas.text: Under pure axial load the concrete and steel act together: the concrete carries 0.85 f'_{c} on the net concrete area and the steel carries its yield strength on its own area.

ideas.title: ACI 318

sections.deep:
Reinforced concrete combines concrete, strong in compression, with steel that carries the tension. At nominal flexural strength the concrete compression is modelled as a rectangular stress block of intensity 0.85 f'_{c} and depth a. Setting the compression equal to the steel tension A_{s} f_{y} gives a, and the moment strength is the tension force times the lever arm d - a/2.

Design strength is the strength reduction factor times nominal strength: 0.90 for tension-controlled flexure and 0.75 for shear. A section is tension-controlled when the steel strain at nominal strength is at least 0.005, which makes the failure ductile and gives warning. Shear is carried by the concrete and by stirrups. Columns are checked with axial load and moment together on an interaction diagram.
method: Compute a = A_{s} f_{y} / (0.85 f'_{c} b).
Compute M_{n} = A_{s} f_{y} (d - a/2).
Apply the strength reduction factor.
Compare with the factored moment from the load combinations.
For shear, compute the concrete contribution and add the stirrup contribution if needed.

terms: couple
two equal and opposite forces a distance apart; together they only turn an object and do not push it anywhere
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
design strength
nominal strength multiplied by a resistance factor less than 1; it must be at least the factored load effect
nominal
calculated from the code formula before any safety factor is applied
stirrup
a bent bar looped around the main steel of a concrete beam to resist shear
stress block
the rectangle that replaces the real curved compression stress in a concrete beam, to make the calculation simple
strain
change in length divided by original length; it has no units
factored
multiplied by a load factor greater than 1, to give a design load with a safety margin
equilibrium
the state of an object that is not accelerating: all forces on it cancel, and so do all their turning effects
yield strength
the stress at which a metal stops springing back and starts to deform permanently
